newsitem.title: INDIA: India's telecom, postal workers go on strike.
newsitem.headline: India's telecom, postal workers go on strike.

text.p: Some one million Indian telephone and postal workers launched a nationwide strike over a wage dispute on Wednesday, partially disrupting operations in the country's financial markets.
The government said postal services could be hit but telecommunications were unlikely to suffer.

"Telecommunications will not be much affected as most of the phone exchanges are automatic but the postal services are likely to be adversely affected," Pradip Bhatnagar, a senior ministry official, told Reuters.
In Bombay, the nation's financial centre, stock markets were not affected by the strike but some banks were hit, dealers said.

Dealers said the stir, which affected local phone lines, hit trading in the interbank call money and securities markets and pushed up borrowing rates. Call rates rose to 10.0 percent in the afternoon from 8.75 percent at the start, dealers said.
"Borrowers were desperate to cover their position," a dealer at a state-run bank said. "Few lenders could be reached."

Mallikarjun (one name), secretary-general of the Bharatiya (Indian) Telecom Employees Federation, told Reuters in New Delhi that striking workers were demanding the abolition of a ceiling imposed by the government on annual bonus payments.
Communications minister Beni Prasad Verma, a socialist, told a news conference that the government sympathised with workers' demands but called the strike illegal.
"It's an illegal strike as they did not even give a 14-day notice to the government (under the law)," Verma said.
New Delhi normally pays most junior employees an annual bonus during the Hindu festive season in October which is usually higher than the previous year.
However, the government this year decided not to revise the payment upwards for its telecommunication and postal employees in 1996 as part of an austerity programme.
Mallikarjun said the employees were upset as the government had revised the bonus allowance for railway workers but left out the telecommunication sector from the benefit.

"I am sympathetic to them and our efforts are fully in the direction that our employees should not have any step-motherly treatment compared to other departments. I am committed to avoid injustice," Verma said in a written appeal to the workers.
But Bhatnagar said bonus payments were linked to productivity, which differed between departments.
Mallikarjun said the strike was total. "Now the ball is in their court. Let the government decide and consider the demands of post and telegraph workers," he said.

In June last year, Indian authorities called out troops to restore disrupted telephone services during a five-day strike by around 450,000 telecommunication workers against the government's moves to end a state monopoly on telephones.

The government had then threatened to fire striking workers. But the strike ended a day after the Supreme Court upheld the government's tenders to invite the participation of private firms in telephone services.
